title: Market structure and ranges

inOneLine.simple: Market structure is the pattern of swings. When an uptrend makes a lower low, its structure is broken and you stop calling it an uptrend.
inOneLine.balanced: [[market-structure|Structure]] has three states: higher highs and lows, lower highs and lows, or overlapping swings in a range. A break of structure changes the description. It does not predict the next move.

explain.simple: Once you have marked the swings, you can describe the chart in one of three ways. Rising swings: an uptrend. Falling swings: a downtrend. Swings that stay between a similar top and a similar bottom: a range. When an uptrend falls below its last higher low, the up pattern is broken. That does not mean price will now fall. It means the old description no longer fits, and you wait for new swings.
explain.balanced: A range has a ceiling and a floor that price has turned from more than once. Its height is ceiling minus floor. In a range, trend tools tend to give poor readings, because price keeps reversing. A break of structure can be followed by a new trend the other way, by a range, or by the old trend resuming. On a shorter [[timeframe]] you will see many small breaks of structure inside one longer swing.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD H4 chart in an uptrend
Last higher lows: 1.09850, then 1.10100. Last swing high: 1.10600
Price then falls and an H4 candle closes at 1.10000
steps: The last higher low was 1.10100. The close at 1.10000 is below it by 1.10100 − 1.10000 = 10 pips.
Price has made a lower low, so the uptrend structure is broken.
The right description now is "uptrend broken, direction unclear", not "downtrend".
A downtrend description would need a lower high as well. Wait to see where the next swing high forms compared with 1.10600.
The highs differ by at most 1.27050 − 1.26980 = 7 pips. The lows differ by at most 1.26040 − 1.25970 = 7 pips.
Neither the highs nor the lows step clearly one way, so this is a range.
Calling this an uptrend because the second high was 5 pips higher would ignore the mixed lows.

explainSimpler: Rising steps, falling steps, or a box. When the steps stop matching, the old label stops fitting.
commonMistake: Treating a break of structure as a signal that price will reverse. Often price only moves sideways, or the old trend resumes. Another mistake is calling a tiny difference between swing highs a "higher high" when the swings really overlap.

quickCheck.prompt: In an uptrend, the last higher low is 1.08500. A candle closes at 1.08420. What has happened?

options.explanation: Right: price closed 8 pips below the last higher low, which is a lower low.

options.text: A downtrend is now confirmed by the lower low
options.explanation: No: a downtrend also needs a lower high. For now the direction is unclear.
No: a lower low breaks the higher-low pattern.

quickCheck.prompt: Swing highs sit near 1.3000 and swing lows near 1.2900, again and again. How do you describe this?

options.explanation: No: the highs and lows are not rising; they keep returning to the same levels.
No: the highs and lows are not falling; the lows keep holding near 1.2900.

quickCheck.prompt: After a break of structure, which of these can happen next? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Right, it can, but it is only one of the possibilities.
Right: price often moves sideways after a break.
Right: the break can turn out to be a pause.

options.text: None of these: a break always leads to a reversal
options.explanation: No: a break of structure guarantees nothing about what comes next.

doItNow.instructions: Start a replay on the strong uptrend scenario. Mark each new swing low as it forms. Pause when a candle closes below the last higher low, and write "structure broken" with the price. Then keep going and note what happened next: new downtrend, range, or uptrend resumed.
